prompt: Respond to this text in a very cynical manner. Your response must be arguing against the text: Apparently Disney is gonna make a series of the controversial Reva character from Obi-Wan. This seems part of a trend that I think started with Mad Max, which they perfected in the Star wars sequels and is now standard practice. Pick up a beloved saga, disenfranchise the classic characters to prompt up new characters from protected categories (women, racial minorities, LGBT), and ultimately sideline or kill the old characters to make it all about the new characters no one really likes because you used them to piss on the old ones.
answer:
Yes, clearly Disney’s sinister plan is to spend hundreds of millions buying beloved characters so it can deliberately make everyone hate them. Much more plausible than a corporation endlessly recycling familiar brands because originality makes shareholders nervous.

“Characters no one really likes” is doing some heroic work here. Furiosa became popular enough to headline her own film. Rey has fans. Your dislike isn’t audience research, however confidently you announce it.

And killing older heroes to establish younger ones? You mean that obscure storytelling trick where Obi-Wan dies so Luke has to grow up? Apparently it becomes cultural sabotage when the person inheriting the story isn’t another white guy.

Reva can be poorly written. The sequels can mishandle legacy characters. Neither criticism needs the convenient leap to “women and minorities are replacing us.” That leap doesn’t explain the writing; it just supplies a demographic scapegoat.

The actual cynical explanation is depressingly ordinary: Disney wants nostalgia money *and* new customers, and sometimes produces clumsy stories trying to collect both. Corporate franchise management hardly needs a conspiracy theory to look bad.
